task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-14, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR (sequential play-type context)
sequential premium relative to a baseline
heterogeneity across player and teammate pairs
methodological_questions: Does a preceding teammate drive raise PNR PPP, or is the gap due to lineup, ball-handler or screener quality, or game context?
How is 'preceding' defined: same possession, or the immediately prior possession by the same team?
How reliable are the DRIVE and PNR labels, and are they derived from the outcome?
Does the data give enough exposure to test an effect for any teammate rather than a pooled effect?
Is the effect an artifact of a generic after-success or sequence effect that applies to every play-type pair?

historical_evidence.finding: Descriptive ranking of same-player and teammate X->Y sequences against Y's baseline. Same-player DRIVE->PNR cells are mixed: L. Doncic +0.309 (n=53) and D. Bane -0.324 (n=70, t=-2.7). Top teammate cells run to about +0.4, but with n around 30 and a cut-off note on teammate DRIVE->PN... [prior work] lists limits of label/classification error and small sample, and the failure mechanism is 'E_unclear'.

After the opponent runs play type X, the team's next play type Y scores above Y's baseline. The 'aftershock' replicates across 8 of 8 play types (for example PNR +0.127, n=51,194; DRIVE +0.123). [prior work] cites small sample as a limitation. It concerns opponent plays before the team's own play, not a teammate drive before a PNR.
Star-level suppression by the preceding opponent play type, with cells of n_after 32-95. Recorded failures: no multiplicity correction and thin cells. Risk [source]: DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY.
The rank-1 suppressor varies across players. Deltas are mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control, and an OTHER-label artifact was flagged.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Player-pair and teammate cell-by-cell sequential premium ranking (including DRIVE->PNR)
failed_approaches.why: Small samples and label/classification error as recorded; the mechanism is recorded as unclear and the cells are not hypothesis tests.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranking per-star sequential effects from thin cells
failed_approaches.why: No multiplicity correction; n_after of 32-95 against thousands of baseline possessions.
Deltas within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; an OTHER artifact was flagged.

evidence_establishes: Per-player and per-pair DRIVE->PNR premiums are heterogeneous in sign. Both a large positive (Doncic) and a large negative (Bane, t=-2.7) appear among cells of n of about 50-70 (FAM:[prior work]).
Cell-level sequential analyses in this project have repeatedly run into small samples, uncorrected multiplicity and label error (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).

[prior work] [prior work] shows a generic positive carry-over (+0.12 to +0.13 in every play type) in the next possession's PPP after a prior possession. Any sequence effect must be measured against this generic baseline.
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record is a powered, controlled test of a pooled effect of teammate DRIVE on PNR PPP.
The retrieved text does not show how 'preceding' was defined, or whether the pooled teammate DRIVE->PNR premium is positive.
Nothing retrieved shows that every teammate drive raises PNR PPP, and the Bane cell points against such a universal claim.
[prior work] do not test the effect for seasons 2025-26 or for playoffs.
own_inferences: The word 'any' makes the claim universal. A single contradicting well-powered cell would refute it, but cells of n of about 50 cannot be well powered, so the claim cannot be tested literally. Only a pooled average effect with a heterogeneity estimate can be tested.

If a DRIVE-labeled possession ends in a drive shot, a DRIVE followed by a PNR can only occur across possessions. The effect would then be confounded with the result of the previous possession (made/missed, live ball or transition), and with generic carry-over as in [prior work].
Teams that drive often are likely good offenses with strong ball handlers, so teammate-drive exposure is confounded with player and lineup quality.

Rough power guess: if about 2,000-8,000 drive-preceded PNRs exist against about 50,000 others, the minimum detectable PPP difference is roughly 0.04-0.07 at SD of about 1.15. Pair-level cells would only detect differences above about 0.4. These counts are not in [prior work] and must be verified.
uncertainties: The actual count of PNR possessions with a preceding teammate drive is unknown.
It is unknown whether the derived records allow a within-possession sequence, or only across possessions.
The label error rate of DRIVE and PNR in the derived records is unknown.
The cut-off text of [prior work] may contain a teammate DRIVE->PNR result that I have not read, since I did not call read_family.
Coverage of the incomplete 2025-26 data on the stated date is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have designed a test of a universal effect over player cells. The retrieved records show that cell-level sequential work is underpowered, uncorrected for multiplicity and subject to label error, and that [prior work] shows a generic carry-over. This pushed me to a pooled estimand with a generic-sequence placebo, hierarchical heterogeneity and no claim about 'any' teammate.
